name: Public facilities in the 1% flood area (overlaid)
group: Facilities and roads in hazard zones
plain: How many public facilities in each municipio stand inside FEMA's 1% flood area.
definition: How many of the municipio's fire and EMS stations, police stations, city halls, libraries, public housing developments, power plants, airports and public schools stand inside FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area. coverage.frequency: One snapshot, rebuilt with the build: the flood layer and facility layers as published, and the public schools of school year 2024.

method: facility_exposure.py lays points and lines on FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area (the Special Flood Hazard Area of the observatory's flood layer, flood.geojson; the rule of the exposure series). It is an overlaid figure (decision 107): one published layer laid on another, with nothing assumed. The points are the layers the map draws (fire and EMS stations, police stations, city halls, libraries, public housing developments, power plants, airports) and the public schools open in school year 2024. A point on the edge of a polygon counts as outside. Bridges are left out: a bridge over a river stands in the flood area by design. Library points within 150 m of an open public school may be the same building; both are counted. 234 points that share their coordinates with another point of the same layer (libraries 216, public housing developments 18) are left out: several facilities listed at one address are not where the buildings stand.
source_detail: The observatory's own layers and files: flood.geojson (FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer), the facility layers, traffic_roads.geojson (FHWA HPMS) and the NCES school directory, https://educationdata.urban.org/api/v1/schools/ccd/directory/2024/?fips=72.
how_to_read: In Puerto Rico, 327 of the 2,274 facilities tested stand in the 1% flood area (14.4%): airports and heliports 3 of 17; city halls 10 of 65; fire and ems stations 10 of 94; libraries 145 of 883; police stations 27 of 141; power plants 13 of 68; public housing developments 23 of 144; public schools 96 of 862. Most: Ponce (42), San Juan (32), Carolina (21).
caveats: It says where a building or a road stands, not that it floods: the floor height of a building and the height of a road are not known, and the flood layer is a simplified copy of FEMA's map.
FEMA's 1% area is the regulatory flood map: it does not include sea level rise, and some areas flood that it does not show.

plain: How many public facilities in each municipio stand inside the area 3 ft of sea level rise would flood.
definition: How many of the municipio's fire and EMS stations, police stations, city halls, libraries, public housing developments, power plants, airports and public schools stand inside NOAA's area flooded by 3 ft of sea level rise above today's high tide (connected to the ocean). It says where the building stands today, not when or whether the sea reaches it.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, rebuilt with the build: the hazard maps and facility layers as published, and the public schools of school year 2024.

method: facility_exposure.py lays points and lines on NOAA's extent of 3 ft of sea level rise above mean higher high water, connected to the ocean (the height the observatory's exposure series headline; low-lying areas not connected to the ocean are left out). It is an overlaid figure (decision 107): one published layer laid on another, with nothing assumed. The points are the layers the map draws (fire and EMS stations, police stations, city halls, libraries, public housing developments, power plants, airports) and the public schools open in school year 2024, each with its students. Bridges are left out. 234 points that share their coordinates with another point of the same layer (libraries 216, public housing developments 18) are left out: several facilities listed at one address are not where the buildings stand.
source_detail: The observatory's own layers and files: NOAA's sea level rise extents (cache/slr), the USGS landslide susceptibility tiles (landslide.py), the facility layers, traffic_roads.geojson (FHWA HPMS) and the NCES school directory.
how_to_read: In Puerto Rico, 17 of the 2,274 facilities tested stand in the 3 ft sea level rise area (0.7%): airports and heliports 0 of 17; city halls 0 of 65; fire and ems stations 0 of 94; libraries 12 of 883; police stations 2 of 141; power plants 1 of 68; public housing developments 0 of 144; public schools 2 of 862. Most: Cataño (4), Salinas (3), Cabo Rojo (2).
caveats: It says where a building or road stands today, not when or whether the sea reaches it: NOAA's extent is a picture of a water level, not a forecast, and it does not include waves, storm surge or erosion.
Low-lying areas that 3 ft of sea level rise would leave cut off from the ocean are not counted.
Roads are read every 20 m, so a stretch shorter than that may be missed or counted whole.

name: Public facilities on high landslide susceptibility land (overlaid)
group: Facilities and roads in hazard zones
plain: How many public facilities in each municipio stand on land the USGS rates highly susceptible to landslides.
definition: How many of the municipio's fire and EMS stations, police stations, city halls, libraries, public housing developments, power plants, airports and public schools stand on land the USGS map rates High, Very High or Extremely High for landslides triggered by intense rainfall (the most susceptible 30% of the main island). It says what the ground under it is rated, not that a slide will happen there; Vieques and Culebra are not in the map.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, rebuilt with the build: the hazard maps and facility layers as published, and the public schools of school year 2024.

method: facility_exposure.py reads the USGS map of susceptibility to landslides triggered by intense rainfall (Hughes and Schulz, 2020) under each point, from the same zoom-15 tiles as landslide.py (about 4.5 m a pixel). A point counts when its cell is High, Very High or Extremely High, the most susceptible 30% of the main island. It is an overlaid figure (decision 107). The points are the layers the map draws (fire and EMS stations, police stations, city halls, libraries, public housing developments, power plants, airports) and the public schools open in school year 2024, each with its students. Bridges are left out. 234 points that share their coordinates with another point of the same layer (libraries 216, public housing developments 18) are left out: several facilities listed at one address are not where the buildings stand.
source_detail: The observatory's own layers and files: NOAA's sea level rise extents (cache/slr), the USGS landslide susceptibility tiles (landslide.py), the facility layers, traffic_roads.geojson (FHWA HPMS) and the NCES school directory.
how_to_read: On the main island, 26 of the 2,249 facilities tested stand on High or higher landslide susceptibility land (1.2%): airports and heliports 0 of 14; city halls 0 of 63; fire and ems stations 0 of 92; libraries 23 of 876; police stations 0 of 140; power plants 3 of 66; public housing developments 0 of 143; public schools 0 of 855. Most: Barranquitas (4), Yauco (3), Utuado (3).
caveats: It says what the ground under a building or road is rated, not that a slide will happen there; the map is not a substitute for a site-specific slope-stability study.

A building stands on a levelled pad, and the 5 m map rates the pad by its own gentle slope: the point under a building reads Low far more often than the slope around it. 94% of public schools read Low, while 11.5% of residents (census block points, landslide.py) live on High or higher land. Read a low count as 'the building's own cell is not rated high', not as 'safe from slides': a slope above or below it, or the road to it, may be.
Vieques and Culebra are not in the USGS map: they have no value, and Puerto Rico's figure is of the main island.
2 points of the main island fall on a cell with no class (water or the edge of the map) and count as not high.
Roads are read every 20 m, so a stretch shorter than that may be missed or counted whole.

It says what the ground under it is rated, not that a slide will happen there; Vieques and Culebra are not in the map.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, rebuilt with the build: the hazard maps and facility layers as published, and the public schools of school year 2024.

method: facility_exposure.py reads the USGS map of susceptibility to landslides triggered by intense rainfall (Hughes and Schulz, 2020) under each point, from the same zoom-15 tiles as landslide.py (about 4.5 m a pixel). A point counts when its cell is High, Very High or Extremely High, the most susceptible 30% of the main island. It is an overlaid figure (decision 107). The points are the layers the map draws (fire and EMS stations, police stations, city halls, libraries, public housing developments, power plants, airports) and the public schools open in school year 2024, each with its students. Bridges are left out. 234 points that share their coordinates with another point of the same layer (libraries 216, public housing developments 18) are left out: several facilities listed at one address are not where the buildings stand.
source_detail: The observatory's own layers and files: NOAA's sea level rise extents (cache/slr), the USGS landslide susceptibility tiles (landslide.py), the facility layers, traffic_roads.geojson (FHWA HPMS) and the NCES school directory.
how_to_read: Main island: 1.2%. Highest: Las Marías (18.2%), Barranquitas (14.3%), Patillas (10.5%). A municipio with few facilities moves a lot with one building: read the count beside the share.
caveats: It says what the ground under a building or road is rated, not that a slide will happen there; the map is not a substitute for a site-specific slope-stability study.

A building stands on a levelled pad, and the 5 m map rates the pad by its own gentle slope: the point under a building reads Low far more often than the slope around it. 94% of public schools read Low, while 11.5% of residents (census block points, landslide.py) live on High or higher land. Read a low count as 'the building's own cell is not rated high', not as 'safe from slides': a slope above or below it, or the road to it, may be.
Vieques and Culebra are not in the USGS map: they have no value, and Puerto Rico's figure is of the main island.
2 points of the main island fall on a cell with no class (water or the edge of the map) and count as not high.
Roads are read every 20 m, so a stretch shorter than that may be missed or counted whole.
